archetype.name: Point Guard (check-down heavy)
archetype.definition: A quick-game distributor who wins by avoiding sacks and spreading short throws around Sean Payton's offense, but rarely pushes the ball past the sticks.

report.headline: Winning games, not throws: a short-area passer stuck in neutral on third down
report.take:
Bo Nix is 5-2, and almost none of that is a passing story. His 5.83 yards per attempt ranks 38th of 45, his -0.046 EPA per dropback is 29th, and he is 1.17 yards per attempt under the league average. The Broncos are winning with the league's fourth-best defense by EPA. Nix's job has been to protect the ball, avoid negative plays and finish in the red zone. He has mostly done that, with a 4% sack rate (8th) and six touchdowns on 30 red-zone attempts.

The passing is split in two. From 0-9 air yards he is efficient and accurate: +0.087 EPA per attempt and +3.2 CPOE on 107 throws, which is the core of the offense. Everything around that core leaks. Throws behind the line have cost -11.1 EPA. Beyond 10 air yards he completes 35.2%. Third down is where drives die: -0.45 EPA per play, -31 EPA in total and a 24.6% conversion rate at an average of 7.8 yards to go. That third-down total is far worse than his entire dropback total of -9.5, so his early-down passing has actually been in the black. With an average throw landing 2.74 yards short of the sticks, the third-down problem looks like a play-design and decision issue more than a protection one. The line allows the fewest QB hits in the league.

The career context matters. Low yards per attempt is who he is: he ranked 38th and 39th in his first two seasons. What's new is the efficiency drop. He was +0.089 and +0.105 EPA per play in 2024 and 2025, and his completion rate is down 4.2 points from last year. Oddly, his bad-throw rate improved to 13.3% from 15.2%. That points partly at the receiving end. Courtland Sutton has produced -0.254 EPA per target on 33 targets, while Pat Bryant's +0.95 on 13 looks like a role worth expanding.

The last three games went 3-0 but carried his worst passing, -0.093 EPA per dropback. That stretch includes Seattle's No. 2 defense and a short-week game. Arizona last week was the encouraging version: 10.7 intended air yards and 73 rushing yards. He showed he can still create when he's asked to push the ball and use his legs.

strengths.title: Efficient, accurate short game
strengths.body: From 0-9 air yards he is above expected on completions and positive on EPA, the most-used area of his passing by a wide margin. It fits Payton's timing concepts and his own decisiveness. It has been his floor across three seasons and should hold.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance, clean pocket
strengths.body: He converts pressure into sacks at one of the lowest rates in the league. That has been true every year (7th and 10th in pressure-to-sack rate before this season). The line also allows the fewest hits in football. This is a durable trait, not luck.

strengths.title: Finishing in the red zone
strengths.body: Six of his seven touchdown passes have come inside the 20, with positive EPA there. His two rushing scores add a second goal-line option. The touchdown efficiency on a 30-attempt sample will wobble, but his red-zone work has been solid in past seasons too.

concerns.title: Third down is sinking drives
concerns.body: His third-down passing is in a different tier from the rest of his game, and it accounts for more lost EPA than his whole season. The cause looks structural: he is throwing short of the sticks and not challenging the intermediate middle. Some regression toward his early-down level is likely. A real fix needs more aggressive third-down calls, though.

concerns.title: Nothing works past 10 yards
concerns.body: He is completing under 40% of intermediate throws, 13.7 points below expectation, with two of his three interceptions there. Deep he is at 28.6%. The deep EPA stays slightly positive only because the hits are big. With Sutton struggling, the downfield game has no reliable outlet, and it is the main reason his yards per attempt trails the league.

concerns.title: Screens and ball security leak value
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have lost more EPA than his short game has gained. He has also lost two fumbles, ranking 36th of 45, with six turnover-worthy fumbles. The screen game is a scheme cost. The fumbles are a real habit to watch, given how thin Denver's offensive margin is.

trend.note: His game EPA has swung from -14.4 at Kansas City to +8.4 against Jacksonville. The overall passing level sits in a flat, below-average band; the last three games averaged -0.093 EPA per dropback despite a 3-0 record. Rushing has picked up lately, highlighted by 73 yards at Arizona.

nextGame.headline: Kansas City takes away the short game he lives on
nextGame.body:
This is the worst stylistic matchup on the board for him. Kansas City ranks second in EPA allowed on short throws, exactly where Nix makes his money. It also ranks third and second against opposing WR1s and WR2s, and allows the third-fewest fantasy points and second-fewest touchdowns to quarterbacks. Week 1 at Arrowhead was his worst game of the year, -14.4 EPA with four sacks. The openings are real but narrow. The Chiefs are 21st against deep passes and 30th in sack rate now, so a cleaner pocket and some shots downfield should be available, provided he hits them, which he hasn't this season.

Availability tilts things. Jaylen Waddle, his most-targeted receiver, left the Arizona game with a chest injury and is questionable. Without him, more volume shifts to Sutton, whose targets have been costly, and to Pat Bryant and Evan Engram, who line up with Kansas City's weak spots against WR3s and tight ends. On the other side, the Chiefs are missing tackles Jaylon Moore and Josh Simmons plus Rashee Rice. That sets up Denver's No. 2 pass-rush hit rate, points to a low-scoring, field-position game (total 41.5) and keeps Nix in his low-risk mode.

keyMatchups.title: Short-area passing vs. stingy underneath defense
keyMatchups.body: His best area runs straight into Kansas City's strongest one. If the quick game stalls, he faces more long third downs, his weakest situation. The counter is the deep middle, where the Chiefs have been far more generous.

keyMatchups.title: Secondary targets vs. soft spots
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City has been gashed by WR3s and tight ends, and sees a larger share of tight-end targets than the league norm. Bryant's +0.95 EPA per target comes on just 13 targets, but if Waddle sits, this is the place to feature him and Engram.

keyMatchups.title: Rematch after a Week 1 mess
keyMatchups.body: He was pressured on 27.3% of dropbacks and sacked four times in the opener. Kansas City now rarely gets home, ranking 30th in sack rate, so protection should be better. The question is whether the extra time turns into completions past 10 yards.

nextGame.watch: Whether Denver lets him attack downfield and on third down the way it did at Arizona, or settles for checkdowns into the league's second-best short defense.

restOfSeason.body: Expect more of the same shape with a slightly better middle. His sack avoidance, short accuracy and around 31 attempts a game in a pass-leaning offense are stable. Third-down passing this bad tends to drift back toward a quarterback's overall level, which should lift his EPA toward neutral. The downfield completion rate has room to improve too, given his past seasons. What won't change much is the yards-per-attempt ceiling, since he has never been a big-play passer. The red-zone touchdown rate may cool. A defense this good keeps game scripts close and his volume steady but modest. That makes him a roughly 170-215-yard passer whose fantasy value depends on goal-line touchdowns and how often Payton lets him run, as he did at Arizona.
swingFactors: Waddle's chest injury and who absorbs his targets
How much designed and scramble running Payton keeps calling

confidence.note: Seven games of stable traits match his career, but key splits rest on small samples and Waddle's status is unclear.
